title: Newton's cradle only behaves like the textbook if its balls don't quite touch

cover.alt: A chrome Newton's cradle seen from above: one steel ball swings out to the left while four hang together in a row.

body: Lift one ball of a Newton's cradle and let go: it stops dead, and the ball at the far end flies out. The simple explanation treats this as a chain of two-ball collisions, each handing on all the momentum and energy. That is only exact if the balls start slightly apart. Most real cradles lack that gap, so one impact squeezes several balls at once: the fourth ball twitches outward too and the first rebounds a little. Steel works well because, in a small cradle, it compresses only up to about 30 micrometres and springs back in under 200 microseconds, losing little energy as heat.

slides.alt: A Newton's cradle with five steel balls, filmed from above in slow motion. The ball at one end swings in and strikes the row, the ball at the other end swings out, and this repeats back and forth.
slides.caption: In slow motion, each end ball swings in and strikes the row, and the ball at the far end flies out. The three in the middle barely move.

steps.label: The lifted ball swings down and strikes
The impact squeezes the steel surfaces
A pressure wave runs through the row
The far ball is pushed out and swings up

slides.label: trips back and forth the pressure wave makes through the balls before the last one leaves
slides.text: Sound crosses about 5 cm of steel in 10 microseconds, roughly ten times faster than the whole hand-over from the first ball to the last.

slides.heading: One ball strikes four touching balls

left.label: Textbook
left.text: The striking ball stops dead and only the last ball moves off, with all of its speed.

right.label: Real steel balls
right.text: A model of the squeezed surfaces gives the fourth ball 13% of the speed, and sends the striking ball back at 7%.

slides.question: You lift two balls together and let go. What happens on the other side?
options: One ball flies out twice as fast
slides.explanation: Two swing out. In the simple picture, a tiny gap between the two dropped balls makes the collisions run as two quick chains, one right behind the other.
